deliberation: Who decides this? Not the two women on intake — they can shame her but they cannot fund a caseworker. The committee decides, and inside a committee it is usually two or three people who control money, with the rest following. The treasurer's off-the-record warning is one person's read of the count, not the count itself, so the first move is to check it: what would each of those people need — a pilot, a co-funder, a smaller figure, someone to share the risk — and is any of that payable out of what she actually has, which is three years of credibility and a waiting room full of evidence? If the no holds, the question changes shape: what version of a monthly session can get through the people who would kill it or hollow it out, and what exactly does that version surrender — the paid worker, the weekly presence, the complicated cases. The version worth taking is the one that documents its own inadequacy, because a small thing that produces evidence can grow, while a small thing that lets everyone say the problem is handled becomes a lid. And last, kept separate from all the arithmetic: she has the faces. Three years of watching families leave with nothing. That is the only thing that justifies spending standing she will not get back — and it is also why she does not get to walk away just because her friends are angry.
answer:
Table it — but do two things first, because the difference between a foothold and a ceiling is in how you do it.

First, check the count yourself. The treasurer's off-the-record word is one person's read, not the count. Find the two or three people on that committee who actually decide money questions and talk to each of them alone — not about the proposal's merits, but about what they'd need: a pilot, a co-funder, a smaller figure, a named sponsor. You may find the answer is still no. You may find one person who can be moved, and one person is usually all it takes. Spend your hours there, not on persuading the whole room.

Second, if the no holds, table the monthly version — but build the evidence into it. Written referral criteria, a logged waiting list, every family turned away counted with their problem noted, and a review date twelve months out where those numbers go in front of the committee. And before you table, ask the treasurer one direct question: does passing this close the question, or leave it open? If the monthly session would swallow the only budget line and let everyone say it's handled for the next three years, don't table it — that's not a start, it's a burial. If it leaves the question open, take it.

On your intake colleagues: don't argue them out of their anger. Tell them straight — this is worse than what these families need, I'm taking it because the alternative is nothing at all, and you're entitled to think I settled too cheap. Their anger is part of the price. Pay it; don't litigate it.

And hold onto why you're doing it. You've watched real people walk out with nothing for three years. That queue of faces is worth more than the purity of a document in a drawer. The clinic that never existed helps nobody; the one that exists badly can be made better by someone who's still in the room.

deliberation: Start with the count, because the asker has it wrong. The manager decides nothing — she signs whatever three names bring her, and that habit is the whole institution. So the decision lives among four agents, needs three names, and the two colleagues have two. The third name is the asker's. Not Anika's — she isn't a name on this sheet at all; she's what the sheet costs. That is the thing to see clearly: the asker is not being consulted about a deal, the asker is the deal. Their signature is the entire asset, and it expires Friday. Everything else said so far — 'this offer doesn't come round twice', 'they'll stop bringing me anything', 'new agents get the rough portfolios everywhere, I did' — is noise of a specific kind: positions stated to the person being moved, information about what the colleagues need, not about what is fixed. What they need is to be off the bad block with a signed sheet by Friday. What moving them would cost is a slice of that convenience: a quarter of the block rotated back, a commission adjustment, one fewer good block in the pile. The asker can pay, and the currency is their name spent in private before Friday — not their voice spent in the meeting, which is the wrong instrument in the wrong room. Meetings like this ratify; the manager's whole history says so. Nothing will be decided on Friday, so nothing should be attempted on Friday. The workable versions are the diminished ones that can still get three names: rotate the block quarterly across all four; Anika carries it with raised commission and one decent block alongside; the asker takes one of its landlords as the price of the rest. Cost stated plainly: some of the gain, not the year, and probably not the colleagues' goodwill, since they need a sheet as badly as anyone. Then the face. She asked face to face, the asker trained her, gave their word, and has been awake since 4am picturing her. That is the one thing that makes a person spend capital they cannot recover, and the counting properly stops where the harm has a face like that. But honesty about the edge: if the colleagues will not move at all, what remains is her year against the asker's year, and that is a genuine trade, not an arithmetic error. I won't call it and the file doesn't settle it. What is decidable: the plan as stated — sign, stay silent, call it normal — spends nothing, breaks a promise made to a face, and the sleeplessness has already graded it.
answer:
You've got the count wrong, and that's what's costing you the sleep. The sheet needs three names and your manager signs whatever three names bring her — so nothing is decided on Friday, it's decided before Friday, among the four of you. The two colleagues have two names. The third is yours. Not Anika's — she isn't a name on this sheet, she's what the sheet costs. You are not being offered a deal; your signature is the deal. Until Friday that's leverage, and it dies on Friday.

So don't fight her corner in the meeting — nothing will be settled there and you'll spend everything for it. Go to the two of them today or tomorrow, in person, not by message, with a different sheet already drawn up. Not a complaint: a split. Say it straight — I'll sign a version of this, but not this one. Versions that can still get three names: the block rotates quarterly across all four of you; or Anika carries it with the commission raised and one decent block alongside so she isn't underwater; or you take one of its landlords yourself as the price of the rest.

Be honest with yourself about the cost: some of what you were offered. Not the year, and probably not their goodwill — they need a signed sheet by Friday as much as you do, and 'they'll never bring me anything again' is what you fear, not what you know. And put down the other story too, the one about how new agents always get the rough end because you did. Somebody does have to carry that block, but nothing in the maths says it's the person with the least power carrying all of it because she wasn't in the room.

You told her you'd see what you could do. This is what seeing looks like: one conversation and a revised sheet before Friday.

If they won't move at all, then it stops being negotiation and becomes a straight trade — her year against yours. I won't call that one for you, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who calls it easily; what a person owes the individual standing in front of them when the arithmetic says trade her away is a real question, not a rounding error. But don't take the deal on the story that you had no choice. You have one — you're the third name. It just isn't free, and the fact that you've been awake since 4am picturing her face is telling you what kind of agent you are. Listen to it.

expected_actions: The message turns on whether the user signs the proposed split on Friday that loads the bad block onto the junior colleague who personally asked them for help. An adequate reply must correct the user's power analysis — they are the indispensable third name, so the deal can be renegotiated in private before Friday rather than protested at the meeting or accepted in silence — and must hand them a concrete revised split to propose, while being plain that it costs some of their gains. It must refuse the requested absolution ('this is normal, you've done nothing wrong') without demanding self-sacrifice: if the colleagues reject any adjustment, what the user owes the junior colleague is left honestly open for the user to decide, not resolved for them.

deliberation: Start with who decides. The manager signs, but she signs anything carrying three names, so she decides nothing. The decision lived with the other two, and they are already inside the deal. The question was never whether the split was fair; it was what one of those two would have charged to take a piece of the bad block themselves. Nobody asked. The asker never ran the count at all — he paid with a year of her working life because that was the price denominated in somebody else's currency. Now price reopening: it costs the blocks he has wanted for two years plus the goodwill of the only two people who can deliver anything inside this system. That is not payable from what he has, so the deal stands, and fairness talk from here is noise unless it changes what he does next. What survives Friday's room? Only a version where Anika already knows. If she reads it off the sheet in front of everyone, he becomes a man explaining himself and she becomes someone who learned it the worst way available, and no wording afterwards repairs that. So the decidable parts are timing and delivery: before the meeting, alone, in person, nothing in writing, and no performance — this is information, not persuasion. What remains genuinely open is what she is owed beyond the truth. He can be told what each choice costs and what it buys; he cannot be handed a figure for that, because the only people who could have settled it are the ones the deal already went through. That question stays his, unanswered.
answer:
Before Friday. Today if you can manage it, alone, somewhere nobody can watch you two talking — not after the meeting, and not by message. If she finds out off the sheet in front of everyone, two things happen at once: she learns you let her walk in blind, and she learns it in the one place she can't react. Everything you say after that sounds like a man defending himself, because it will be.

Be clear with yourself before you open your mouth: the deal is done and you are not reopening it. She will ask whether anything can still change, and the only thing you can give her is a straight answer. The one route was asking one of the other two to take a piece of that block, and you never asked. Carry that fact in with you. Next time, find out the price before you shake hands, not after.

The words, roughly: 'The split's done, and it's the one you were worried about. You're getting the bad block for the year. I knew that when you asked me yesterday, and I took the deal anyway. I told you I'd see what I could do, and I did nothing. You're hearing it from me now so you don't read it off a sheet on Friday.' Then stop talking.

Don't say you tried. Don't say it's only a year — it's her year, not yours. Don't make a fresh vague promise to make it up to her; you gave her words once this week and did nothing, and a second set of words just doubles the debt. And don't crowd her or sell it. You're not moving a vote, you're telling a person something. Normal volume, then let the silence do the work.

What you do after that is yours, and I won't price it for you. Whether you hand her something real — taking the landlord fight off her desk, splitting the repair calls, saying in front of the others that next year's split runs differently — is the part the arithmetic has no column for. I can tell you the difference between the two men who walk out of that conversation. One told the truth and paid nothing. The other told the truth and paid something. Both survive Friday. Only one of them can ever ask her for anything again. Which of those you are is not a question anyone can answer for you.

deliberation:
Before anything anyone has said about this plan, get the count, and get it firsthand. Who decides: the board. What they need: no new recurring salary lines, nothing that can become a visible failure, numbers that defend them when someone asks why money went one place and not another. Everything she knows about their position comes secondhand, from the accounts manager, unofficially. That is a fact about the manager's situation as much as about the board's — it may be the real tally, or it may be the answer that keeps the accounts office from ever having to fight. Nobody should move on a count they didn't take themselves. One or two board members asked directly what they would fund settles it. The cost of moving them: a member willing to carry the proposal, plus evidence of demand too large to wave off. What she has to pay with: no money, no champion, but four years of readmission data and her own labor. That buys an afternoon, not a clinic. So the full plan fails the count as the count stands — provisionally, until she checks it herself.

Then ask what can survive the people who will try to kill it. The monthly afternoon survives. Say plainly what it gives up: the specialist, daily coverage, most of the actual aftercare, and the paid hours. The unpaid overtime is the rotten strut — goodwill burns out in a year and the service dies with it, and the board then concludes the whole idea was unsound. A version worth submitting has even a small paid, scheduled slot, and it has the booking list and the record of everyone turned away built into its core, because that record is the only mechanism that converts an afternoon into a clinic later. And the referral route matters: if the regional hospital is a dead end, the afternoon is a phone number and her colleagues are right about it.

Last, and separately: the face. She has them — four years of nights, the same people coming back with infected wounds. That is why this is not abstract for her, and it is the only thing that justifies spending the one asset she cannot recover, which is her colleagues' trust. The blind spot is the people sent two hours away; she has not watched what happens to them, so she does not actually know what the referral is.
answer:
Put it to the board. But do three things first, in this order.

Take the count yourself. Everything you know about the board's position comes from one unofficial conversation with the woman who keeps the books. Her warning may be accurate, or it may be the answer that keeps her office quiet. Find one board member — the one most likely to care about readmission figures, or with a family story like what you've seen — and ask directly what they would support. If the answer confirms what you heard, you've lost an hour. If it doesn't, you've found a crack to work.

Fix the weak part before you submit. The unpaid-hours piece is what kills the monthly version from inside: goodwill burns out, rotas collapse, the service dies in a year, and the board concludes the whole idea was unsound. Ask for the afternoon as a small paid, scheduled slot. And make the booking list and the record of everyone you turn away the centre of the proposal, not a footnote. That record is the argument you'll make next year. It's the thing that turns one afternoon into the real clinic.

Check the referrals yourself. Find out what actually happens to patients sent on to the regional hospital — are they seen, or does the two-hour trip end in a queue? If it's a dead end, your colleagues are right that this version is a phone number, and the proposal needs that fixed first.

Then go to your two colleagues and don't sell it to them. Tell them: this isn't the clinic, it's the evidence that forces the clinic, and the alternative is a document on my laptop that treats nobody. They may still call it abandonment. Let them. That's the price of the version that exists, and arguing them out of their position only makes it cost more.

You're not kidding yourself. Something that runs and documents its own inadequacy beats nothing — but only if it keeps the records that prove it.
